intro: Thirty-six verses of victory procession, and the hardest Hebrew in the book. Something like a dozen words here occur nowhere else in the Bible, several more occur only in forms nobody can parse with confidence, and the ancient translators were already guessing at them. Read it as a march: God goes out from Sinai, crosses the wilderness, scatters kings, chooses a mountain over the taller ones and sits down on it, and the last third is the parade arriving at the sanctuary with singers in front, drummers in the middle and foreign envoys bringing tribute at the back. Many rites say it on Shavuot, on the strength of verse 19. The one thing to notice while learning it: how often these notes have to say that a word is uncertain. That is not caution on this page, it is the condition of the text.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster. Of David.
A psalm, a song.

verses.summary: Two genre words stacked at the end, psalm and song, which is unusual and tells the performer this is music for a procession rather than for private prayer.

stichs.en: Let God arise,
let His enemies be scattered,
and let those who hate Him flee from before Him.

verses.summary: The opening is a rewriting of the words spoken whenever the ark set out, in Numbers 10:35. There it is an imperative addressed to God; here it is a third person wish, and the divine name has been changed. The psalm starts by quoting the moment a march begins.

stichs.en: As smoke is driven off, so drive them off;
as wax melts before fire,
let the wicked perish before God.

verses.summary: Two images of something that cannot hold its shape, and both verbs of dissolution are passive or intransitive. Nothing is described as being fought. The enemy simply stops being able to stay solid.

stichs.en: But the righteous will rejoice,
they will exult before God,
and they will be glad with gladness.

verses.summary: Three verbs of joy against the three verbs of dissolution in the verse before. The last one takes a noun from its own root, a Hebrew way of intensifying that English can only render as be glad with gladness.

stichs.en: Sing to God, make music to His name,
build a road for the One who rides through the desert plains;
Yah is His name, and exult before Him.

verses.summary: The verb glossed build a road for is the one used of clearing and raising a highway, so the singing is itself the roadwork. The word after it, given here as desert plains, is contested and carries the whole picture with it; see the remez.

stichs.en: Father of orphans and judge of widows
is God in His holy dwelling.

verses.summary: The storm rider is defined by two legal roles at the bottom of the social scale. Judge of widows means the one who takes their case, not the one who tries them.

stichs.en: God settles the solitary in a home,
brings prisoners out into prosperity;
only the rebellious dwell in a scorched land.

verses.summary: The word rendered into prosperity occurs only here and nobody knows what it means. Proposals include good fortune, singing, and at the right season. The sentence works whichever is chosen, which is why the guess has survived so long.

stichs.en: O God, when You went out before Your people,
when You marched through the wasteland. Selah.

verses.summary: Two infinitives with the suffix Your, one clause each, and no main verb until the next verse. The grammar leaves the sentence hanging on purpose while the earth answers it.

stichs.en: the earth quaked,
the heavens too poured down before God,
this Sinai,
before God, the God of Israel.

verses.summary: The two words given here as this Sinai sit in the line with nothing attaching them grammatically to what surrounds them. Read as a demonstrative they are an aside pointing at the mountain; read as an old relative pronoun, which some Semitic languages have, they make a title, the One of Sinai.

stichs.en: A rain of free gifts You shook down, O God;
Your inheritance, when it was weary, You Yourself set firm.

verses.summary: Rain of free gifts uses the word for a voluntary offering, so the downpour is described as a donation rather than as weather. The second half is compressed to the point of ambiguity: it is not certain whether the inheritance is the land or the people.

stichs.en: Your living company settled in it;
in Your goodness You provide for the poor, O God.

verses.summary: The first word is the ordinary noun for a living creature, in the singular with Your attached, used here for a group. Translations pick flock, troop or community according to whether they read the march as pastoral or military.

stichs.en: The Lord gives the word;
the women who bring the news are a great army.

verses.summary: The participle for those who bring the news is feminine plural, so the messengers of victory are women, as in the songs of Miriam and Deborah. English translations that write heralds erase the grammar; the ending is unambiguous.

stichs.en: Kings of armies flee, they flee;
and she who stays at the house divides the spoil.

verses.summary: The verb is repeated with no conjunction, which in Hebrew reads as continuous action, running and running. The woman at home dividing the plunder is the last word of a battle report, and the phrase behind she who abides is not certain; some read it as the beauty of the house.

stichs.en: When you lie down among the sheepfolds,
the wings of a dove are sheathed in silver,
her pinions in yellow-green gold.

verses.summary: One of the least understood verses in the psalter. The word given here as sheepfolds is a dual noun that appears in one other place and may mean sheepfolds, saddlebags or ash heaps, and nobody can say how the silver dove follows from lying down among them. The image is beautiful and the sentence is broken.

stichs.en: When Shaddai scattered kings in it,
it snowed on Zalmon.

verses.summary: Snow on a dark wooded hill, immediately after scattered kings. Whether the snow is a picture of the whitened bones of a defeated army, or of drifting fugitives, or simply a change of weather marking the event, the verse does not say.

stichs.en: A mountain of God is the mountain of Bashan,
a mountain of many peaks is the mountain of Bashan.

verses.summary: The word mountain four times in eight words. Mountain of God here works as a superlative, an enormous mountain, and the compliment is set up only so that the next verse can take it away.

stichs.en: Why do you look on with envy, you many-peaked mountains,
at the mountain God desired for His seat?
The LORD will dwell there forever.

verses.summary: The whole argument of the middle of the psalm: the chosen mountain is not the tallest one. The verb glossed look with envy occurs only here and is guessed at from context, look askance, watch resentfully, or possibly leap about.

stichs.en: The chariotry of God is twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands;
the Lord is among them, Sinai in holiness.

verses.summary: The last word of the count appears nowhere else in the Bible. Thousands upon thousands renders the guess that it comes from a root meaning to repeat; readings taking it as a place, a class of angels or a scribal slip have all been proposed. The second line is four words with no verb in it.

stichs.en: You went up to the height, You took captives,
You took gifts among men,
even from rebels, so that Yah God might dwell there.

verses.summary: The best known verse of the psalm, and the reason it is read on Shavuot. The Hebrew says gifts were taken, not given; the direction of the exchange is part of what the later readings argue about. See the drash.

stichs.en: Blessed is the Lord,
day by day He carries the load for us,
the God who is our deliverance. Selah.

verses.summary: The verb in the middle is the one used for loading a pack animal, and the preposition after it can mean for us or onto us. So the line reads either He carries our burden or He loads us up, and both have been defended. Day by day is a doubled noun, the Hebrew way of saying every single day.

stichs.en: The God for us is a God of deliverances,
and to the LORD, the Lord, belong the ways out from death.

verses.summary: Deliverances is plural, which reads as repeated rescues rather than one final one. The last word means exits or outlets, the same noun used for the boundary points of a territory, so death is described as a place with doors that belong to someone else.

stichs.en: Surely God will smash the head of His enemies,
the hairy crown of the one who walks on in his guilt.

verses.summary: The march turns violent again. The participle glossed walks on is the reflexive form used for going about one's business, so the enemy is not caught fighting but caught continuing, which is the point of the line.

stichs.en: The Lord said:
From Bashan I will bring back, I will bring back
from the depths of the sea,

verses.summary: Bashan is the high ground of verse 16 and the sea depths are its opposite, so the pair means from the top of the world to the bottom of it. What gets brought back is not stated, and translations supply either the enemy or the exiles.

stichs.en: so that your foot may smash through blood,
the tongue of your dogs have its portion from the enemies.

verses.summary: The same verb as in verse 22, now with a human subject. The last word is obscure and the line has been read as wade rather than smash on the strength of a similar-looking root; either way this is the most brutal image in the psalm, and it is addressed to the listener, not to God.

stichs.en: They have seen Your processions, O God,
the processions of my God, my King, into the sanctuary.

verses.summary: The camera turns. Everything up to here was reported; from here it is watched, and the noun repeated twice is the plural of a word for a way of walking, so what is seen is the gait of the procession rather than its destination.

stichs.en: Singers went in front,
players behind,
among young women beating hand drums.

verses.summary: The order of the parade, given as a stage direction with no verb in the middle clause. The drummers are the same instrument and the same social role as the women at the Sea in Exodus 15:20.

stichs.en: In assemblies bless God, the Lord,
you who are from Israel's fountain.

verses.summary: Fountain of Israel is a metaphor for descent, the spring a people flows from. The line is what the procession is chanting, quoted inside the description of it.

stichs.en: There is Benjamin, the youngest, leading them,
the princes of Judah in their throng,
the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.

verses.summary: Four tribes only, two from the south and two from the far north, standing for the whole. The word glossed their throng occurs once in the Bible and its meaning is unknown; throng, council and shouting have all been proposed.

stichs.en: Your God has commanded your strength;
show strength, O God,
You who have acted for us.

verses.summary: The first three words can be pointed as a statement, your God has ordained your strength, or as an imperative addressed to God, command Your strength. The versions split on it, and the difference decides who is being asked for something in this verse.

stichs.en: From Your temple above Jerusalem,
kings will bring You tribute.

verses.summary: The march has arrived, and the direction of traffic reverses: until now God has been coming in, from here the nations come in. Tribute is a single short word, the formal term for a present brought to a sovereign.

stichs.en: Rebuke the beast of the reeds,
the herd of bulls among the calves of the peoples,
trampling on pieces of silver.
He has scattered the peoples who delight in battles.

verses.summary: The most damaged verse in the psalm. The beast of the reeds is usually taken as a marsh animal standing for Egypt, the bulls and calves as rulers and their followers, and the two words before silver are so uncertain that translations range from submitting himself to trampling to scattering.

stichs.en: Envoys will come out of Egypt;
Cush will hurry to stretch out its hands to God.

verses.summary: The word glossed envoys occurs only here. Envoys is a guess supported by similar-looking words in neighbouring languages; bronze objects and nobles have also been proposed. Cush is the region south of Egypt, along the upper Nile.

stichs.en: Kingdoms of the earth,
sing to God, make music to the Lord. Selah.

verses.summary: The two imperatives of verse 5 come back, addressed now to the kingdoms rather than to Israel. The psalm closes by handing its own opening line to everyone else.

stichs.en: to the One who rides the highest heavens, the ancient ones;
behold, He sounds His voice, a voice of power.

verses.summary: The rider of verse 5 returns, and this time the place he rides is unambiguous, the heavens of heavens. That the doubtful word in verse 5 gets replaced here by a clear one is itself an argument in the dispute over what it meant.

stichs.en: Ascribe strength to God;
His majesty is over Israel,
and His strength in the clouds.

verses.summary: Give strength to God is not a contribution but an acknowledgement, the same idiom as in Psalm 29. The verse divides the territory: majesty over one people, strength across the sky.

stichs.en: Awesome is God from Your sanctuaries;
the God of Israel, He gives strength and might to the people.
Blessed is God.

verses.summary: The strength the congregation was told to ascribe in the verse before is handed straight back to them here, by the same noun. The psalm ends on two words, blessed and God, which is as short as a closing formula gets.

pardes.body: A march in three movements. Verses 2 to 11 are the departure: God rises, the enemy dissolves, the column goes out through the wilderness and the mountain shakes. Verses 12 to 24 are the campaign: kings run, spoil is divided, a mountain is chosen and occupied, captives and tribute are taken. Verses 25 to 36 are the arrival, and the pace changes completely, because now the poem is describing something being watched rather than something being done. Singers in front, instrumentalists behind, drummers in the middle, four tribes named, then envoys from Egypt and Cush, then the kingdoms of the earth told to sing the same two verbs Israel was told to sing in verse 5. Read the geography and the argument is plain: the movement is from Sinai to Jerusalem, from a mountain in the desert to a smaller hill that was chosen over taller ones, and the whole psalm exists to say that the God of the wilderness now has an address.

This is the hardest text in the Psalter and the honest report is a list of unsolved words. The largest is {{5.6}} in the call to prepare a road for the rider. The Masoretic pointing gives the plural of the noun for desert plain, and the sense is then the One who rides through the steppes, which fits a psalm about crossing a wilderness. A second reading takes it as a cognate of the word for cloud found in Ugaritic poetry, where the storm god carries the standing title rider of the clouds, and reads the One who rides the clouds. Verse 34 gives the same participle with an unambiguous sky word, which is evidence for the cloud reading; verse 8 gives the desert with an unambiguous word, which is evidence for the other. Neither is decisive. Around it sit words that occur once and are guessed from context: {{7.6}}, {{17.1}}, {{18.4}}, {{28.6}}, {{32.1}}. And {{9.7}} with {{9.8}} may be a demonstrative, this Sinai, or an archaic relative particle of the kind Arabic still has, giving the One of Sinai as a title. When a translation of this psalm reads smoothly, that fluency was added by the translator.

Verse 19 carries most of the later reading. You went up to the height, you took captive, you took gifts among men: the Talmud reads the ascent as Moses going up Sinai and the gifts as the Torah, brought down to human beings over the objection of the angels, and this is why the psalm is attached to Shavuot in the rites that assign it there. Note what the reading does with the grammar. The Hebrew says gifts were received, and the midrashic reading turns the receiving into a delivery, on the argument that what Moses took he took in order to give. Verse 28 has its own history: the Talmud brings it into the dispute about which tribe went into the Reed Sea first, dividing {{28.3}} into two words so that Benjamin the youngest is not ruling them but going down to the sea. Verse 6, father of orphans and judge of widows, is the verse most often quoted from this psalm outside of any of that, and it is quoted for itself.

The Talmud's list of the seven heavens takes the name of the highest, Aravot, from {{5.6}} of this psalm, reading the rider not as crossing a desert but as enthroned above the outermost firmament, where justice and righteousness and the treasuries of life are stored. That is the mystical resolution of the philological problem in the remez: the obscure word is not decided between desert and cloud, it is read as the proper name of a place that is neither. On that reading the psalm's whole geography becomes vertical. The going out of verse 8 and the going up of verse 19 are one movement seen from two ends, and the mountain God desired for a seat in verse 17 is the point where the highest heaven touches a specific hill that is not the tallest one available. The chosen thing being smaller than its rivals is the recurring shape here, and the kabbalistic tradition treats it as the rule rather than the exception: a vessel receives in proportion to how little it insists on its own height.
